title: How neuromorphic computing and silicon photonics could cut computing energy — and what’s stopping UK success
label: 4 November 2026 · Low-energy computing evidence session
summary: Industry experts explained how brain-like (‘neuromorphic’) computing and silicon photonics can cut energy use, speed up time‑critical AI and let devices compute at the edge. They gave concrete examples (event cameras, memristors, integrated photonic chips), said the UK has world-class research but lacks the scale, foundry access and patient capital to commercialise it, and set out practical asks: a pilot manufacturing line, Government help to get university IP into big foundries, and procurement or diplomacy to anchor the sector.

glossary.definition: Hardware and chips that are designed to work like biological brains, often with memory and computing co-located.
A neural model that encodes signals as time-based spikes, allowing event-driven, low-energy processing.
Using light (photons) on silicon chips to move and process data more efficiently than electrons alone.
A factory (eg TSMC, GlobalFoundries) that mass-manufactures semiconductor chips from customers' designs.
A device whose electrical behaviour depends on past signals; can act as memory and computation in one.
A shared mid-scale manufacturing facility that proves a design can be made reliably before mass production.
Resistive random-access memory, a type of non-volatile memory useful for co-locating memory and compute.
A sensor that only outputs changes in a scene, producing far less data than full-frame cameras.

chapters.title: What the technologies are and why they matter
chapters.takeaway: Neuromorphic chips emulate brain-style, event-driven processing and silicon photonics uses light to move lots of data with low energy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re looking at low-energy computing — neuromorphic computing and silicon photonics — and how they might be turned into real products.

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: Analogue neuromorphic uses hardware that behaves like spiking neural networks, so it’s event-driven and can learn or adapt in real time rather than only in big offline training runs.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: Neuromorphic borrows from the brain: it co-locates memory and compute and pays attention only to useful signals. Combined with photonics, it lets us handle some problems at much higher speed.

turns.speaker: Freddie van Mierlo
turns.text: Quickly — what is silicon photonics in plain terms?

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: Photonics is light-based technology; silicon photonics puts light paths on small chips so you can transmit huge volumes of data using much less energy than electrons over wires.

turns.speaker: Dr Josh Silverstone
turns.text: I build photonic neuromorphic systems for time-critical tasks — finance, defence, robotics — where nanoseconds and power efficiency matter.

chapters.title: Concrete benefits and examples
chapters.takeaway: These approaches promise orders-of-magnitude energy savings and new, fast edge capabilities — examples include event cameras, memristor sensors and integrated photonic chips.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: People often compare brains (about 20 W) to data centres (hundreds of kilowatts to megawatts) — can these technologies really narrow that gap?

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: Yes. Data centre energy is often spent moving and storing volatile data. Neuromorphic chips combine memory and compute, cut data movement and use spikes to send only important information.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: An event camera only reports pixels that change, so you avoid digitising an entire image. If you scale that idea to other sensors, you avoid generating vast amounts of useless data.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: Memristors can be light-sensitive, store information and compute locally — imagine an artificial retina where sensing, memory and processing sit on the same plane.

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: Silicon photonics already moves hundreds of gigabits per second on tiny chips. That reduces energy per bit and is essential as AI demand balloons.

turns.speaker: Dr Josh Silverstone
turns.text: Our focus is latency-sensitive inference: fusion control, satellite links, robotics — places where faster, more efficient answers are commercially valuable today.

chapters.title: Main barriers: scale, foundries, investment and coordination
chapters.takeaway: The UK has top research and early companies but lacks mid-scale manufacturing, easy foundry access, patient capital and a co‑ordinating strategy to commercialise.

turns.speaker: Maya Ellis
turns.text: You say the UK has IP and research — why hasn’t it turned into big commercial firms?

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: A big bottleneck is foundries. Big global fabs (TSMC, UMC, GlobalFoundries) control the manufacturing 'recipes'. UK research can’t get easy access to those recipes to commercialise.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: There’s also a funding and risk‑appetite gap. A rule of thumb from the witnesses: roughly $100m is often needed to move from lab tech to commercial silicon — that needs patient private capital plus public support.

turns.speaker: Kit Malthouse
turns.text: Why does value sit with foundries and not with designers like we have in the UK?

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: You can capture value by getting your IP into mass manufacture at the big foundries — but you need Government or a national body to open those doors and negotiate access.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: We also need an ecosystem: pilot lines, testbeds, design tools, packaging and importantly procurement pull from Government to be early customers.

turns.speaker: Daniel Zeichner
turns.text: Does the UK have the industrial capacity to manufacture at commercial scale?

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: No single country does the full advanced stack — it’s global. But the UK can own parts: design, materials, pilot manufacture and niche foundries for edge chips.

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: Smaller UK foundries like Pragmatic and Paragraf can make chips for edge use-cases. That gives a form of sovereignty if we coordinate and fund scale-up.

turns.speaker: Tom Collins
turns.text: Is ASML-level equipment needed here? That’s a decades-long, hugely expensive effort.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: ASML's extreme‑ultraviolet machines are unique and cost hundreds of millions — we don’t need to chase that for photonics. Photonics works at larger device scales and needs different tools.

chapters.title: Practical asks: pilot lines, diplomacy, procurement and capital
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses asked for a UK pilot manufacturing line, Government to help negotiate foundry access, more patient capital and procurement to anchor demand.

turns.speaker: Kit Malthouse
turns.text: Who should be the 'guiding mind' inside Government to coordinate this — UKRI, the UK Semiconductor Centre?

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: The UK Semiconductor Centre exists for this. We need it to take authority to negotiate with big foundries and make university IP accessible for manufacture.

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: Our survey of ~100 UK photonics companies points at a clear gap: proving manufacturability at pilot scale. A national pilot line would let companies go from 1 prototype to thousands of wafers.

turns.speaker: Daniel Zeichner
turns.text: What scale for a pilot line?

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: Industry estimates: roughly 10,000–20,000 wafers a year; building one might take 3–4 years and could generate significant economic impact by the mid-2030s.

turns.speaker: Dr Josh Silverstone
turns.text: To compress timelines to 2–3 years for productisation would need roughly £100m of capital for ventures like ours — we’ve currently raised about £10m to date.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is £20m government funding to 2030 enough to deliver sovereign capability?

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: No — £20m seeds activity but won’t deliver sovereign commercial capability. Moving lab tech to foundry-scale needs far more sustained funding and patient private investment.

turns.speaker: Martin Wrigley
turns.text: What about the risk of big companies like Nvidia buying the tech and moving value overseas?

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: That can happen. The defence is to back UK firms (eg Fractile) to use the IP so the value sits with home companies, and to create infrastructure that anchors jobs and R&D here.

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: Infrastructure can anchor multinational investment — Microsoft bought a UK photonics spin-out but built nearby facilities to keep talent and R&D local.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the short asks are: a time‑bound feasibility for a pilot line, Government help to open foundry doors, more patient capital and procurement to be early customer?

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: Yes, and include neuromorphic in national strategies, fund testbeds, and consider doctoral training and workforce development for the field.

turns.speaker: Dr Josh Silverstone
turns.text: Also, aim higher on ambition: if we want global companies formed here, be willing to back big projects and international partnerships rather than only tiny bets.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you — this gives the Committee concrete policy levers to consider.
